name: Nabota

lead: Nabota is a botulinum toxin type A from Daewoong of South Korea, sold in the US as Jeuveau. People use it to smooth frown lines and crow's feet, and it is also discussed for slimming the masseter muscle to narrow the lower face and for calf contouring.

It blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, weakening the injected muscle temporarily so wrinkles soften or bulk reduces. It has been studied in glabellar and crow's feet lines, masseter hypertrophy, calf contouring, post-stroke spasticity and blepharospasm, including comparisons against Botox.

paras: A clinician injects the target muscles in a short visit, and people repeat treatments as the effect wears off over a few months. Wrinkle use is the established route; jaw slimming is an off-label use that tends to show over weeks as the muscle shrinks.

It is prescription-only and the effect is temporary. Reviews note that repeated exposure to any foreign protein can provoke immune responses and that evidence on the purity and immunogenicity of newer formulations is limited.

angle.text: Nabota, sold as Jeuveau in the US, smooths frown lines and is also used to slim the masseter for a narrower lower face. The toxin relaxes the targeted muscles so wrinkles soften and bulk reduces. Wrinkle use has trial support, while jaw slimming appears in smaller reports and is largely off-label.

lead: Nabota (prabotulinumtoxinA) is a botulinum toxin type A made by Daewoong Pharmaceutical of South Korea.[1][2] Injected into chosen facial muscles by a clinician, it relaxes them for a few months, which smooths frown lines and crow's feet and, in the lower face, can slim a bulky masseter so the jawline looks narrower and more tapered.[3][4][5] The same toxin is marketed in the US as Jeuveau, sold by Evolus and manufactured by Daewoong, according to Wikipedia.[6]

Beyond wrinkle treatment, it has been studied in post-stroke spasticity, blepharospasm, myofascial pain and calf contouring.[7][8][9] Aesthetic uses sit within the much larger field of botulinum toxin cosmetics, which a 2023 narrative review calls the most popular cosmetic procedure worldwide, with applications from the glabella to masseters, chin and gummy smiles.[10]

Two approaches to the lower face illustrate how the same product serves different looks. In the upper face, clinicians inject small amounts to flatten frown and crow's-feet lines. In the jaw, they inject larger amounts into the masseter, and in the 2024 placebo-controlled phase 3 trial of prabotulinumtoxinA the greatest reduction in muscle thickness was seen at 12 weeks, with differences from placebo at every time point [11].
Reviews note that published evidence on the purity and immunogenicity of newer toxin formulations such as Nabota is limited.[1]

paras: Cosmetic uses studied include glabellar lines in a phase 4 single-arm study,[4] masseter reduction in a split-face comparison with Botox,[3] and calf contouring in a pilot comparison.[5] Narrative reviews of toxin aesthetics describe muscles targeted for contour as well as lines: bulky masseters, cobblestone chin, gummy smile and downturned mouth corners.[10]

Masseter treatment is the use most relevant to jawline appearance. Enlarged masseters give some faces a square lower third, and toxin-induced thinning of the muscle is used to soften that shape; calf slimming follows the same logic and is discussed mainly in East Asian literature.[3][5]

A phase 3 trial randomized 197 patients with post-stroke upper limb spasticity to Nabota or Botox,[7] a phase 4 follow-up has been published,[12] and a pilot study examined cervical and shoulder myofascial pain.[8] A registered phase 2/3 trial covers essential blepharospasm.[9]

Like other type A toxins, it blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, so the injected muscle contracts less until nerve endings recover.[6] Formulations differ in manufacturing process, accessory proteins and excipients; a 2018 comparison of Asian formulations noted that essential formulation data are not always public.[2]

Daewoong's product was developed as an alternative to the original Botox (onabotulinumtoxinA), whose commercial history began with Oculinum Inc. and its acquisition by Allergan.[6] Early publications on Nabota date from 2015 (post-stroke spasticity) and 2017-2018 (masseter, calf and glabellar studies).[7][3][4][5] In the US it is sold under the name Jeuveau by Evolus, and under the name Nuceiva in some other markets.[6] Wikipedia lists Jeuveau/Nuceiva alongside Botox Cosmetic, Dysport and Xeomin as the commercial cosmetic toxins.[6]

All botulinum toxin products carry class-wide cautions. Wikipedia's botulinum toxin article records that in 2008 the FDA warned the toxin can spread from the injection site and weaken unintended muscles, especially in children with cerebral palsy, and that in 2009 the agency announced boxed warnings about distant spread and renamed several products [6]. Cosmetic use is described there as able to cause unintended facial muscle weakness, difficulty swallowing, headache, flu-like symptoms and allergic reactions, with bruising attributed to the injection itself [6].

The 2023 narrative review lists FDA-approved cosmetic toxins including prabotulinumtoxinA alongside onabotulinumtoxinA, abobotulinumtoxinA, incobotulinumtoxinA, letibotulinumtoxinA, daxibotulinumtoxinA and rimabotulinumtoxinB, and presents consensus practitioner guidance on injection points that differs between Asian and Caucasian patients [10].

Head-to-head data come mostly from non-inferiority designs. The post-stroke spasticity trial randomized 99 patients to Nabota and 98 to Botox [7]. In aesthetics, a split-face masseter study compared Nabota with Botox on opposite sides of the same face [3], and the calf-contouring pilot compared the two formulations in muscular calves, a concern described as common among Asian women [5]. The phase 2 duration trial randomized 154 adults (mean age 47) to 40 units of prabotulinumtoxinA, or 20 units of prabotulinumtoxinA or onabotulinumtoxinA, using Kaplan-Meier duration of effect for glabellar lines as the primary endpoint [13].

A 2020 review of neurotoxin impurities said Nabota/Jeuveau, Meditoxin/Neuronox and Botulax contain nontoxic accessory proteins and excipients, that any non-human protein can provoke immune reactions with repeated use, and that clinical evidence on purity and treatment failure is limited.[1] A 2021 review of toxin immunogenicity similarly describes antibody formation after long-term repeated use as a possible cause of clinical non-response, and notes that formulations have evolved toward fewer unnecessary components.[14]

Reported adverse events in the trials below were generally mild; the masseter phase 3 trial reported no serious adverse events over 48 weeks.[11] As with all botulinum toxins, injections are prescription-only and performed by trained clinicians.

A Cochrane systematic review pooled randomized trials with more than 50 participants comparing botulinum toxin A products with placebo, other toxins or hyaluronic acid fillers, with participant-assessed success and major adverse events such as eyelid ptosis as primary outcomes [15].

Masseter: a double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial randomized 180 patients to saline or prabotulinumtoxinA (48 units) and measured masseter thickness, 3D imaging and a hypertrophy scale. The largest differences from baseline appeared at 12 weeks, differences between groups were significant at all time points, and no serious adverse event occurred. An open-label extension ran to 48 weeks.[11] An earlier split-face study compared two formulations for masseter reduction.[3]

Wrinkles: a single-arm phase 4 study examined Nabota for glabellar lines,[4] and the US programme for prabotulinumtoxinA-xvfs produced phase 3 post hoc analyses in men, in patients with skin of color and in millennials, plus repeat-dose phase 2 safety studies.[16][17][18][19] A 154-patient phase 2 trial compared a 40-unit dose with 20-unit prabotulinumtoxinA and onabotulinumtoxinA controls for duration of effect.[13] A Cochrane review pooled randomized trials of botulinum toxin A products for facial wrinkles.[15]

Other: the post-stroke spasticity phase 3 trial (197 patients) compared Nabota with Botox,[7] and a pilot compared formulations for calf contouring.[5] Registered trials include a phase 2/3 study in crow's feet lines (n=238), a phase 3 study in benign masseteric hypertrophy (n=180), a phase 2/3 study in blepharospasm (n=234) and a phase 4 comparison with onabotulinumtoxinA for facial wrinkles (n=26).[20][21][9][22]
